2.10 Model adequacy: band-limited posterior predictive calibration and a subject-level test

The calibration of Sections 2.2-2.3 concerns parameter recovery (prior self-consistency on synthetic data). Real data require a second check: for each subject we drew 48 parameter sets from the posterior by weight, simulated, computed the 15 statistics, and asked whether the observed value falls inside its 95 % posterior predictive interval (Figure 11).

Choice of test.

Pooling the 15 ×117 = 1755 posterior predictive p-values into a single KS test (D = 0.239, p ≈ 5 × 10 ⁸⁹) is not appropriate here, because the 15 statistics of one subject are strongly dependent, so ⁻ the degrees of freedom of that test are severely overestimated and the number is uninterpretable. We therefore use: per-statistic coverage with exact (Clopper-Pearson) intervals, per-statistic KS uniformity tests (BH-corrected), a subject-level clustered bootstrap and a Monte-Carlo test. Table 13 gives the perstatistic outcome, and the same quantities are shown as coverage and departure-from-uniformity panels in Figure 11.

The result is a restrictive but actionable finding: mean per-statistic coverage is only 0.758 (subject-level clustered bootstrap 95 % CI 0.725-0.791; median per-subject coverage 0.80), and 12 of the 15 per-statistic p-value distributions depart significantly from uniformity (BH q < 0.05). The structure is clear: • Inter-regional imaginary coherency: iCOH_DMN_SN (0.949) is compatible with nominal; but iCOH_DMN_AN (0.991) and iCOH_SN_AN (1.000) show over-coverage, i.e. prediction intervals that are too wide and therefore under-discriminative -also a form of misfit, invisible in a coverage number alone, which is why we report the KS test as well.

• Alpha band and DMN_delta: AN_alpha 0.889 (KS q = 0.106, marginally usable), DMN_delta 0.846, SN_alpha 0.812.

• Theta/delta/beta relative powers are systematically too narrow: AN_theta 0.410, SN_theta 0.581, DMN_beta 0.650.

The reading is that the model class explicitly parameterises an alpha resonance and inter-regional coupling, so per-subject predictions of those statistics are trustworthy, whereas low-frequency (theta/delta) and high-frequency (beta) relative powers are not directly constrained by the model's mechanism and are not reproduced subject by subject. This bounds the inference: the E/I-derived quantities, resonance frequencies and coupling indices are reportable, while the claim that the model reproduces a participant's full spectrum is not. We treat this as an actionable result, because it identifies where the model must be extended -for instance with slow inhibitory adaptation or a thalamo-cortical loop to constrain the theta band -and we confirm with a random split of the cohort into halves (coverage 0.764 vs 0.753) that the verdict is stable in sample.

3. Discussion

>Discussion

3.1 Main findings

In eyes-closed resting-state EEG from 117 participants, amortised Bayesian inversion of a three-region excitatory-inhibitory network model gave three headline results. First, depression was accompanied by a shift towards excitation in all three networks studied, the default-mode network, the salience network and an anterior frontopolar node, together with a stronger inhibitory loop gain and a lower operating-point drive; the intervals of five derived quantities excluded zero, and the direction survived alternative definitions of the control group and a symptom-dimension contrast. This is what the E/I imbalance hypothesis predicts at the macroscopic level [7] [8] [9], and it is the first cohort-level test of that prediction to rest on a model whose derived quantities have been calibrated individually. Second, the model-inferred default-mode rhythm frequency rose with symptom severity, while the conventional alpha peak frequency measured from the same recordings did not (partial rho = 0.54 controlling case status); the association is not significant among the 11 participants with current MDD, so its robustness is limited by subsample size and it requires replication in a larger sample [20, 22]. Third, we mapped the boundaries. At the state level, sample-by-sample tracking is bounded by the model's intrinsic stochasticity (r about 0.63, with an oraclenoise upper bound of 0.73), whereas sudden shifts of the operating point are detected within milliseconds, which is the quantity a controller actually needs. Closed-loop stimulation, compared against a dosematched open loop, gave no accuracy advantage, so we claim real-time feasibility and the potential of a state-adaptive dose, but not an accuracy gain.

3.2 Methodological contributions

1. A constructive fix for the ill-posed prior, with a reproducible metric. Independent sampling of gains leaves only 2.4 % of draws usable and makes 61.2 % of them saddles; the stable frequency parameterisation raises the acceptance rate to 30.3 % and reduces the saddle fraction to 0.

2. Calibrated amortised inference. One library of 1.2 × 10⁵ simulations served 117 participants at an amortisation ratio of ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵, with coverage near 0.95 for K ≥ 250 and N ≥ 3 × 10⁴, and with conclusions that do not drift with the hyper-parameters; the conclusion is additionally verified under three independent frequency priors, end to end. We also report the negative result that the locallinear adjustment inflates the bias to +4.5 and the coverage to 0.31, which is why it is off by default, and which illustrates the general point that a regression-adjusted estimator need not improve on the plain one [50, 72].

3. An honest identifiability report covering the derived quantities, not only the free parameters.

Although the resonance frequencies contract only by 0.11-0.22, their recovery coverage is 0.96-1.00 with correlations of 0.84-0.88; the loop gain has a negative contraction and is therefore restricted to group-level statements and never interpreted individually.

4. Quantifying the observability ceiling instead of reporting a flattering tracking coefficient.

The mean skill score is 0.045, and we state explicitly that sample-by-sample reconstruction is not achievable; an oracle-noise ablation pins the ceiling at 0.7-0.9.

5. A negative result we keep.

The apparent dose efficiency of closed-loop stimulation does not survive a dose-matched comparison. We report it as a negative result rather than retaining a "positive" conclusion that depends on an inappropriate baseline. 6. A band-limited adequacy statement. Posterior predictive checks show well-calibrated statistics (iCOH, alpha power) coexisting with systematic misfit (theta/delta/beta relative power), which delimits what this model class may be used to claim.

3.3 Relation to previous work

The E/I imbalance hypothesis predicts excitation dominance in depression [7] [8] [9]. Our results are consistent with it at the level of macroscopic network dynamics, and they connect the spectroscopy literature to EEG: if cortical E/I shifts, the network-level signature should be a change in balance and in the strength of inhibitory feedback, which is what we observe. The non-parametric route to E/I from field potentials [14, 15] provides the natural benchmark, and we find that the two families have comparable discriminative power under a common criterion, a result that should temper the assumption that mechanism buys accuracy. Spectral parameterisation tools [16] and the aperiodic-exponent literature [17] [18] [19] are complementary rather than competing: they describe the spectrum without committing to a mechanism, and our band-limited misfit, in which theta, delta and beta relative powers are not reproduced, says that the two should be combined rather than opposed.

Within the modelling literature, this work sits between the neural-mass and whole-brain traditions. The WC model and its descendants supply the local dynamics [27] [28] [29] [30] [31]; DCM concentrates on a small number of subjects with subject-specific optimisation and model comparison [32] [33] [34] [35] [36] 78]; and whole-brain modelling has begun to address clinical stratification and the role of the E/I ratio [37] [38] [39] 42, 43]. Our contribution is not a new model but a scalable inversion of an existing one, together with the calibration evidence that amortised inference requires. Methodologically this is an instance of simulation-based inference at cohort scale [49, 55], and it inherits the validation obligations of that field [58, 59, 72, 73, 79, 80]. Where likelihood-free methods have been applied to neural-mass models before, it has either been to a single system [48, 56] or with neural density estimators [54, 57]; the weighted-neighbour form used here [45, 47, 50, 52] is the simplest variant that delivers calibrated intervals at this scale.

The closed-loop component connects to two literatures. Non-invasive rhythmic stimulation can entrain cortical oscillations [60] [61] [62], and closed-loop paradigms have produced clinical gains in essential tremor and in working memory [64, 65], while invasive stimulation is established in refractory depression [63]. Our negative dose-matched result is a caution for that field: the apparent advantage of feedback may come from the choice of a fixed-amplitude baseline rather than from feedback itself, and comparisons should be dose matched. Finally, our reproducibility practice follows the open-code norms of the computationalneuroscience community [81] [82] [83], and it uses the established Python scientific stack [84] [85] [86].

3.4 Limitations

1. Band-limited adequacy (Section 2.10): per-subject theta/delta/beta relative powers are not reproduced, and inferences resting on them are not supported; prediction intervals for inter-regional coherency are too wide [73, 80].

2. No discriminative advantage (Section 2.6): the aperiodic exponent matches the model-derived quantities in effect size (AUC difference 0.001 [-0.162, 0.156]), so we make no claim of model superiority.

3. Limited power: with n = 22 versus 95 the minimum detectable g is ≈ 0.67, so the three E/I group contrasts should be treated as exploratory [87, 88]. 4. Control-group composition: 86 of 117 participants had no SCID interview, and 9 subthreshold participants (mean BDI 23.1) were included in the control arm. The sensitivity analysis confirms that the direction is robust, but a strict case-control design requires a larger sample.

5.

Restricted population: the cohort is 18-24 years old, so the conclusions are confined to late adolescence and early adulthood. 6. Spatial reduction: only 12 channels were downloaded (FZ, P1, PZ, P2, FC1, FCZ, FC2, AF3, AF4, O1, OZ, O2, used as network proxies plus an occipital reference); no average reference was applied, no source reconstruction was performed and no lead field was modelled; averaging within a network ignores heterogeneity. Representing the third network by AF3/AF4 stretches construct validityits anterior part is available, but the parietal nodes of the canonical frontoparietal control network are missing (P1/PZ/P2 were assigned to the DMN). We therefore relabel it the anterior frontopolar node (AN) and present its results only as evidence about an anterior network [83]. 7. Identifiability: wII and the inter-regional couplings are weakly identified, and the loop gain has a non-positive contraction, so its individual values are not interpreted. 8. Model simplifications: τ, θ and σ are fixed; there are no conduction delays and no thalamo-cortical loop; the absolute value of f scales with τ (S2 Data); and the closed-loop results remain simulation evidence without validation in real stimulation [56]. 9. The absolute scale of the observation is not identifiable: EEG amplitude is arbitrary and the observation gain and noise are partly collinear, so the absolute level of the latent state cannot be recovered from a single recording. We therefore standardise each signal to the subject's own model E fluctuation scale and centre it on its operating point, which makes the observer an estimator of deviations from the operating point, and take the control target from the measured pre-perturbation operating point. 10. Constructed nature of the synthetic validation: the observer benchmark injects a known slow drive, so it tests whether a state that does carry information can be tracked, not whether all resting-state dynamics are explained by this model. 11. Further limitation of the closed-loop control: a fixed open-loop amplitude u = 0.55 equal to the perturbation amplitude implicitly encodes prior knowledge of that amplitude; if the perturbation amplitude varies between trials the controller would have to be retuned. The dose-matched comparison exposes the baseline dependence of the efficiency claim, but we did not run an experiment with a mismatched perturbation amplitude, which we leave to future work.

3.5 Concluding remarks

We established and validated a complete, reproducible pipeline -three-region Wilson-Cowan modelling, a stable frequency-parameterised prior, amortised ABC inversion, group statistics with bootstrap uncertainty and a power analysis, posterior predictive adequacy checks at the subject level, real-time state estimation and closed-loop stimulation simulation -and we report three of its boundaries: identifiability (gains and loop gain are weakly identified, whereas the resonance frequencies are well calibrated), observability (tracking capped at 0.7-0.9 while operating-point detection takes 8 ms) and adequacy (lowfrequency band powers are not reproduced). Applied to public depression EEG, the method reveals a consistent E/I shift and elevated loop gain across three core networks, plus a severity-related network resonance frequency. What is directly reusable is the modular structure of the pipeline, its calibration evidence, and the limits it makes explicit, including one negative conclusion that we kept. We see the honest reporting of those limits as part of the contribution rather than as a caveat [38, 49, 82].

4. Materials and methods

>Materials and methods

4.1 Data and preprocessing

Data. OpenNeuro dataset ds003478 (*EEG: Depression rest*) [89], containing resting-state EEG of depressed and control participants in alternating ~66 s eyes-closed/eyes-open blocks at 500 Hz, 64 EEG + 2 EOG channels, with BDI, STAI, SCID and HamD clinical scales.

Channel selection.

To keep the download tractable (HTTP range requests) we selected 12 channels in advance as network proxies: FZ, P1, PZ, P2 (DMN), FC1, FCZ, FC2 (SN/dACC), AF3, AF4 (anterior frontopolar), and O1, OZ, O2 (occipital reference, used for the aperiodic exponent and peak-frequency descriptors). This choice was made before the data were inspected, but it does limit spatial resolution (Section 3.4, item 6).

Inclusion.

Eyes-closed segments of 117 participants were successfully retrieved and preprocessed (mean 191 s, median 195 s). The archive stores the raw data in a time-major layout (not the conventional channel-major EEGLAB layout); reading it as channel-major introduces spectral comb artefacts at 15/30/45 Hz, so we parse it as time-major. Preprocessing (code/02_preprocess.py, built on the MNE-Python, NumPy and SciPy stacks [84] [85] [86] and organised along BIDS lines [83]): (1) eyes-open/closed decoding from event values (odd = closed), keeping eyes-closed segments only; (2) despiking by robust median/MAD z-scores with linear interpolation of flagged runs up to 25 samples; (3) ocular regression on HEOG including ±60 ms lagged copies; (4) 0.5-45 Hz zero-phase FIR band-pass plus a 60 Hz notch; (5) resampling 500 → 250 Hz; (6) rejection of 1 s windows whose power exceeds median + 6•MAD. VEOG was unusable and dropped. Data are used with the dataset's original reference (no re-referencing).

Regional time series.

Channels were averaged within functional networks (Table 14).

4.2 Three-region Wilson-Cowan model

For region i {DMN, SN, AN}: with S the logistic sigmoid shown above, fixed tau_E = 10 ms, tau_I = 20 ms, theta = 3, and noise intensity sigma = 0.05.

The readout is the excitatory activity y_i = E_i. C_ij denotes the excitatory projection from region j to region i (6 free couplings). There are 15 free parameters: 3 x wEE, 3 x wEI, wIE, wII, 6 x C, and the operating-point offset Delta. Integration uses vectorised RK4 (dt = 1 ms); 4 s of burn-in precede 15 s of analysis, output decimated to 250 Hz [27] [28] [29] [30].

4.3 Stable frequency parameterisation of the prior

We do not sample gains; the operating point and the resonance frequency are explicit prior parameters.

(a) Operating point. Let the target excitatory activity be E* = S(θ + Δ) with Δ sampled so that E* ∈ [0.25, 0.65] (near the inflection of the sigmoid, where the gain S′ is maximal). The inhibitory fixed point I* solves the self-consistency equation x + wII•S(x) = wIE•E* (vectorised bisection), I* = S(x). The tonic drive is then recovered as The determinant therefore equals σ² + ω² > 0 while the trace remains < 0: every sample is a stable focus, and "whether it oscillates" is decoupled from "how fast". Note that f_i is itself not a free parameter but the target used to construct wEI_i; its posterior distribution is induced from the posterior over the 15 parameters through Eq (5) (code/04_fit.py::_res_freq).

(d) Validity screening.

The full 6 × 6 Jacobian is assembled and samples whose largest eigenvalue has a non-negative real part are rejected (inter-regional coupling can still destabilise the network); we additionally require S′_I > 0.06 and physiologically plausible gains. The acceptance rate is about 30.3 % (Table 1).

4.4 Summary statistics

Absolute power depends on skull thickness, electrode impedance, the reference and the unknown lead field and cannot be reproduced by the model, so only spectral shape is matched [14] [15] [16]. Model and data are summarised by the same function, giving a 15-dimensional vector: • 12 band log relative powers: log(band power / broadband 1-30 Hz) for δ(1-4), θ(4-8), α(8-13) and β(13-30) Hz in each of the three regions; • 3 alpha-band imaginary coherences: mean |Im coherency| over 8-13 Hz for DMN-SN, DMN-AN and SN-AN, which are insensitive to zero-lag volume conduction.

|Im coherency| carries a positive finite-sample bias √(1/(πL)) with L the number of averaged segments; the analytic null value is subtracted from both model and data.

4.5 Amortised approximate Bayesian computation

Estimator. Weighted k-nearest-neighbour ABC [44, 45, 47, 52, 53]. A single prior-predictive library of N = 1.2 × 10⁵ pairs (θ_i, s_i) is generated once. For each subject, distances are computed in MAD-standardised summary space, the K = 250 nearest neighbours are retained, and the Epanechnikov kernel w_i = 1 -(d_i/d_(K))² defines the weighted posterior sample {θ_k, w_k}.

On the local-linear adjustment.

The regression adjustment of Beaumont and colleagues [45, 50] is off by default: on 80 pseudo-subjects it raises the wEE bias to +4.51 with an MSE/variance of 5.03 and a coverage of 0.31 (Table 4), whereas the plain weighted-neighbour posterior is calibrated (bias ≈ 0, MSE/variance ≤ 1).

Calibration validation.

Eighty pseudo-subjects drawn from the prior are inverted with the identical pipeline, reporting bias, MSE/variance, correlation and 95 % coverage, in the spirit of simulation-based calibration [58, 59, 79]; the same battery is applied to every derived quantity (EI_i, f_i, loop gain, drive offset) as well (Table 3).

4.6 Hyper-parameters, prior specification and computational benchmarks

Hyper-parameter sensitivity. On a fixed set of pseudo-subjects (fixed seed) the recovery validation is repeated for K {60, 120, 250, 500, 1000} and for libraries subsampled to N {3 × 10⁴, 6 × 10⁴, 1.2 × ∈ ∈ 10⁵}; in parallel, the group effect sizes of the real cohort are recomputed at each K to test whether the biological conclusion drifts.

Prior-specification robustness. Three frequency priors -f logU(2.5, 16) (this work), logU (1, 20) and ∼ logU(4, 14) -are each used to build a 3 × 10⁴ library, and all 117 participants are re-inferred end to end with the same K and the same summary statistics; group effect sizes and the f_DMN-versus-HamD association are then compared.

Performance. We measure (i) the cost of one prior-predictive simulation (average over 512 draws), (ii) the extrapolated build time of the 1.2 × 10⁵ library on one and eight cores, (iii) the per-subject and fullcohort ABC query times, and (iv) the particle filter's compute time per second of data (1500 particles, 20 s of synthetic data). The amortisation ratio is the library build time divided by the per-subject inference time. All times are wall-clock and are taken from the reference run recorded in S8 Data.

4.7 Group comparisons, symptom associations and uncertainty

Derived quantities: the E/I balance index EI_i = log10(wEE_i/wEI_i); the inhibitory loop gain g_loop = √(wIE•wII); the operating-point drive offset Δ; the per-region analytic resonance frequencies f_i; and the six inter-regional couplings C_ij.

Group comparison: lifetime MDD (current or past, n = 22) versus non-MDD (n = 95), Mann-Whitney U with Hedges g, plus age/sex-adjusted OLS (HC1 robust standard errors), BH-FDR corrected [74] [75] [76] [77].

Control-definition sensitivity additionally uses four alternative control definitions and one symptomdimension definition (Table 7).

Symptom associations: Spearman correlations and partial correlations (controlling age and sex; the f_DMN row additionally controls case status) of every quantity with BDI, STAI and HamD, reported stratified by interview subsample (Table 9).

Uncertainty: every effect size and correlation is accompanied by a 95 % percentile interval from 2000 subject-level bootstrap resamples; the AUC intervals come from the same bootstrap.

Power: achieved power and the minimum detectable effect size at a given n are computed from a noncentral t approximation; we report them because small samples are a known threat to the reliability of neuroscience findings [87, 88].

Sample note:

participant sub-064 has no recorded age; models and bootstraps that include age or sex use n = 116.

4.8 Model-free baseline comparison

To ask what the model adds, ten model-free descriptors (aperiodic exponents in three regions, alpha peak frequencies, alpha relative powers, total power) are compared with five model-derived quantities under a common criterion: group Hedges g, AUC (converted from the Mann-Whitney U), FDR-corrected q, and each marker's Spearman correlation with HamD/BDI, including bootstrap intervals and within-family FDR [26, 79]. We also report a paired-bootstrap interval for the AUC difference between the best model-derived quantity and the best descriptor.

4.9 Posterior predictive adequacy check

For each subject, 48 parameter sets are drawn from the posterior (the 250 weighted neighbours) by weight, simulated, and reduced to the 15 statistics. For each statistic we test whether the observed value falls inside the 95 % posterior predictive interval (with exact intervals for the coverage [90]) and run a perstatistic KS uniformity test (BH-corrected). We add a subject-level clustered bootstrap of the coverage, a Monte-Carlo test against the independent Bernoulli(0.95) null, and a stability check on a random split of the cohort into halves. A pooled KS test over 15 × 117 dependent p-values is avoided here, because its degrees of freedom would be severely overstated [58, 59, 80]. The step is complementary to the recovery validation of Section 4.5: the latter tests the estimator's calibration on synthetic data, the former the model's adequacy on real data.

4.10 Bayesian state observer

The state is x = (E_1..3, I_1..3); the dynamics are the WC equations at the subject's posterior-median parameters, and the observation is the three regional signals y_t = g•E_t + n_t. The key design choice is to make the latent state genuinely trackable: without an input the model sits essentially at its fixed point, so any observer would be evaluating noise fitting rather than tracking, an uninformative benchmark. Synthetic validation therefore injects a known slow drive (0.12-0.65 Hz sinusoid, amplitude 0.15-0.60) so that E_t follows a structured deterministic trajectory, with 40 % relative observation noise added. The signal is expressed in latent units (g = 1) and only the observation noise σ is profiled -by maximising the one-step predictive log-likelihood on the first 25 % of the record, with the Gaussian normalising constant included (otherwise σ saturates at the grid's upper bound) -and then frozen for the held-out window. The bootstrap filter [67] [68] [69] [70] uses 1500 particles initialised at the model's own operating point (E*, I*). Reported metrics: state RMSE, skill = 1 -RMSE/baseline relative to the mean-only baseline, E/I state correlations, ESS and resampling rate. Detection latency is the time from a drive step until the filtered estimate first crosses "pre-step mean + 2 SD". A separate oracle-σ ablation bounds tracking performance. Because real EEG has neither ground truth nor an absolute scale, each subject's signals are first standardised to that subject's model E fluctuation scale and centred on its operating point E* (with g = 1) before σ is profiled.

4.11 Closed-loop stimulation simulation, dose-matched control and dose efficiency

Three conditions (no stimulation, fixed-amplitude open loop, closed loop) share one noise realisation. The first 20 % of each trial is unperturbed and its mean defines the healthy operating point used as the control target; a pathological drop of 0.55 in tonic drive is then applied, and the conditions differ only in how they stimulate. The observation is g•E plus noise (g = 8) and the target is the mean excitatory activity across regions. The closed loop runs the particle filter (800 particles) on the most recent 0.6 s of observation every 0.1 s and sets the stimulation amplitude to u = clip(2.5•(E*_healthy -Ê), 0, 0.8); the open loop applies a fixed amplitude after the perturbation. The controller uses only prior-centre parameters and does not know the subject's true parameters. We compare the steady-state error (final 20 s), the dose ∫|u|dt and the fraction of time within ±10 % of the target, using paired Wilcoxon tests, and report the error reduction per unit dose; the controller and the dose-matching logic follow standard feedback-systems practice [91].

Dose-matched control.

For each trial the open-loop amplitude is solved from the closed-loop dose as u_match = dose_closed / (0.8 • T_total), so that the two arms deliver the same dose; an open-loop gradient at u = 0.10, 0.20 and 0.35 is added to trace the dose-error curve (code/17_dose_matched.py). All conditions reuse the same per-trial seeds, so the noise realisations are paired.

4.12 Software, data and reproducibility

All code is Python 3.13 (numpy, scipy, statsmodels, matplotlib [85, 86]), numbered by stage: 01 data acquisition → 02 preprocessing → 03 features → 04 ABC inversion → 05 statistics → 06 observer → 07 closed loop → 08 main figures → 10 analyses → 11 figures → 12 consistency check → 13 severity-marker comparison → 15 derived-quantity, power and control-definition analyses → 16 estimator variants and τ sensitivity → 17 dose-matched control → 18 additional figures. Random seeds are fixed explicitly. The prior-predictive library and the per-subject posteriors ship with the package, so every result can be reproduced without re-running the simulation campaign (code/run_all.sh). A cell-by-cell comparison of a full re-run against the archived tables, and a check of every number quoted in this manuscript against the result files, are recorded in docs/复现与一致性核对_261013.md and shipped as S1 Text and S9 Data. The third node is published as AN; the analysis code identifies it internally as RN, and every shipped table carries the published label (code/_labels_an.py). Regenerating a table directly from results/ therefore yields the same numbers under the legacy identifier RN. The whole chain is version-controlled and shipped with the data that it reads, following open-science practice [81-83].

Figure 3. Parameter-recovery validation (80 pseudo-subjects, identical pipeline).

Figure 4.

Figure 4. Identifiability of the derived quantities. A: prior-to-posterior contraction (red: the loop gain, whose contraction is negative). B: synthetic recovery coverage and correlation for the same quantities (dashed line: nominal 0.95).

Figure 5.

Figure 5. Estimator sensitivity and computational performance. A: recovery coverage versus the number of neighbours K. B: coverage versus prior-predictive library size. C: group effect sizes versus K (the biological conclusion is stable). D: computational cost breakdown (log scale).

Figure 6.

Figure 6. Prior-specification robustness. A: group effect sizes under the three frequency priors. B: Spearman correlation of f_DMN (blue) and paf_DMN (red) with HamD.

Figure 7.

Figure 8.

Figure 8. Inferred quantities versus symptom severity (BDI/STAI/HamD): scatter plots and Spearman correlations.

Figure 9.

Figure 9. Bayesian state observer and closed-loop control. A: observer versus prior-only RMSE on synthetic data. B: detection latency distribution after a drive step. C: steady-state error under the three stimulation conditions. D: true versus filtered latent trajectory for a representative subject (r = 0.90).

Figure 10.

Figure 10. Dose-matched control. A: open-loop dose-error gradient with the closed loop and the dosematched open loop superimposed (the two coincide). B: per-trial closed-loop dose -the closed loop adapts its dose but delivers nothing on 5 of 12 trials.

Figure 11.

Figure 11. Model adequacy. A: per-statistic 95 % posterior predictive coverage with exact intervals (green: KS q ≥ 0.05). B: per-statistic departure from uniformity (BH q).
